nameStory: The bufflehead gets its charming name from its distinctively puffy, rounded head that reminded early observers of a buffalo's bulky noggin. The 'buffalo head' was eventually shortened to bufflehead, though this tiny duck is about as far from a massive bison as you can imagine!
description: The bufflehead is one of New England's smallest and most adorable ducks, roughly the size of a pigeon. Males are striking black-and-white birds with an oversized puffy head that looks almost cartoonish, while females are more subdued grayish-brown with white patches. These compact little sea ducks are excellent divers, disappearing underwater to hunt for small fish and aquatic insects.

idTips.label: Puffy rounded head
idTips.description: Both males and females have distinctively large, rounded heads that look almost too big for their compact bodies - like they're wearing a fluffy winter hat

idTips.label: Male's bold pattern
idTips.description: Breeding males are unmistakable with crisp black backs and brilliant white sides, plus a large white patch wrapping around the back of their puffy black head

idTips.label: Female's white cheek patch
idTips.description: Females are brownish-gray overall but show a distinctive oval white patch on each cheek that stands out against their darker head

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than most other ducks you'll see - about the size of a pigeon and looking almost toy-like on the water

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch them suddenly vanish underwater with a quick forward dive, often staying submerged for 10-20 seconds while hunting

idTips.label: Fast wing beats
idTips.description: In flight, their wings beat incredibly rapidly with a distinctive whistling sound, and they fly low and fast over the water

habitat: Look for buffleheads on calm coastal waters, protected bays, harbors, and large inland lakes during winter months. They prefer areas with depths of 4-20 feet where they can easily dive for food. You'll often spot them in small groups in places like Boston Harbor, Narragansett Bay, or larger lakes like Lake Champlain.

seasonality.spring: Peak viewing time as migrating flocks pass through in March and April. Males display their striking breeding plumage and perform head-bobbing courtship displays.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer as they head north to breed in Canada and Alaska. Any sightings would be exceptional non-breeding birds.
seasonality.fall: First migrants begin arriving in October and November. Mixed flocks of males (some still molting into winter plumage) and females become more common.
seasonality.winter: Best season for reliable viewing from December through February. Both sexes present in harbors and unfrozen coastal waters, with males in full striking plumage.

funFact: Buffleheads are the only ducks small enough to nest in old woodpecker holes! They specifically use cavities made by Northern Flickers, squeezing through entrance holes barely 2.5 inches wide to raise their families in trees near northern lakes.
confusionNotes: Female buffleheads might be confused with female goldeneyes, but buffleheads are much smaller with a more compact, rounded head and smaller white cheek patches. Remember: bufflehead = tiny with a bubble head, goldeneye = larger with a more angular head and bright yellow eyes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sea duck,' buffleheads actually nest in freshwater areas near forests and only move to saltwater during winter. This makes them unique among diving ducks in their seasonal habitat switching.
compareHints: Buffleheads are much smaller than their goldeneye cousins and have that distinctive puffy, rounded head shape. Common Goldeneyes are noticeably larger with more angular heads, bright yellow eyes, and different white markings - males have a round white spot in front of the eye rather than the bufflehead's wrap-around white patch. Barrow's Goldeneyes are extremely rare in New England but would also be larger with a different head shape and white markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Goldeneyes are much larger than their Bufflehead cousins and have different head patterns - males lack the Bufflehead's white head patch that wraps around the back of the head.
Compared to Common Goldeneye, Barrow's has a more triangular white face patch, steeper forehead, and slightly larger overall size.
